title: Particle verbs I: small words, new meanings
title_target: Klart jag kommer ihåg Anna och Lars!
goal: Use the everyday particle verbs — *tycka om, komma ihåg, ta på sig, stänga av, sätta på, hälsa på* — with the stress in the right place and the object after the particle.
bekal: the stress rule: the particle carries the stress (*stänga AV, hälsa PÅ*)
word order: *Jag tycker inte om det* · *Stäng av den!*
telling a particle (*hälsa PÅ* = visit) from a plain preposition (*lyssna på* = listen to)
wave: Go back to Unit 2: say six sentences about your own move or trip, each one starting with a time clause — när, innan, efter att, medan, sedan, tills — and check that the main verb comes straight after it.

notes: **Stänga av, sätta på** — "turn off" and "turn on" (literally "close off", "set on"). In a particle verb the **particle takes the stress** and the verb is said lightly: **steng-ah AHV**, **set-tah POH**. English does the same thing: you say "turn OFF", not "TURN off". If you stress the verb instead, Swedes may hear a different construction altogether.

**Hälsa på** with stress on *på* means "visit": *Mamma och pappa vill hälsa PÅ oss*. Without the particle, **hälsa** means "greet" or "send regards": *Mamma hälsar till dig* — Mom says hi. *Hälsa Ahmad från mig!* — Say hi to Ahmad from me. And with an unstressed *på* it's back to greeting: *Hon HÄLSAR på mig varje morgon* — she says hello to me every morning.

**Lyssna på nyheterna** — here *på* is just a preposition, the way "to" is in "listen to". It stays **unstressed**: **LÜS-nah poh**. The same goes for *titta på* (look at) and *vänta på* (wait for). Rule of thumb: if the small word changes the meaning of the verb, it's a particle and gets the stress; if it simply links the verb to its object, it doesn't.

**Komma ihåg** (**kom-mah i-HOHG**) means "remember". *Ihåg* exists only in this expression, so learn it as a block. **Komma på** is different again: "think of, come up with" — *Varför kom jag inte på det?* (Why didn't I think of that?)

**Tycka om** (**tük-kah OM**) means "like". Watch where *inte* and other adverbs go: **between** the verb and the particle — *Jag tycker **inte** om att diska*, *Han kommer **aldrig** ihåg*, *Jag tyckte **väldigt mycket** om stugan.* On its own, *tycka* means "think, have an opinion" — that's Unit 12.

**Ta på dig mössa** — *ta på sig* (put on clothes) uses a reflexive pronoun that changes with the person: *ta på mig, ta på dig, ta på sig*. Its opposite is *ta av sig* (take off). And a word of warning: use **sätta på** only about machines and lights. With a person as the object it turns into crude slang.

grammars.title: Particle verbs: the particle takes the stress
body: A particle verb is a verb plus a small word — usually an adverb like *av, på, upp, ut, om* — that together form a new meaning. English is full of them (turn off, give up, look out), so the idea is familiar. What you have to learn is which combinations Swedish uses, because they rarely match English one-to-one.
after: Dictionaries sometimes mark the stressed particle with a small sign, e.g. *tycka ´om*. When you learn a new verb with a particle, say it aloud with the stress on the particle three times — that is how it sticks.
In the past and the perfect, only the verb changes: *jag tyckte om, jag har tyckt om; jag stängde av, jag har stängt av*.

grammars.title: Where do inte and the object go?
body: Two rules cover almost everything at this level. **Sentence adverbs** (*inte, aldrig, alltid, bara*) go between the verb and the particle in a main clause. **Objects** — even short pronouns — go **after** the particle.

head: Pattern
Swedish
English
rows: Have you turned off the stove?

after: The second row is where English speakers slip. English puts a pronoun **inside** the particle verb ("turn it off"); Swedish keeps the verb and particle together and puts the pronoun after: *Stäng av den!* — never *Stäng den av*.

head: Words
Plain meaning
Particle-verb meaning
rows: *Ta inte på tavlan!* — Don't touch the painting! (*på* unstressed)
*Ta på dig jackan!* — Put your jacket on! (stress on *på*)
*Se ut genom fönstret!* — Look out the window!
*Du ser trött ut.* — You look tired.
*Han kom på bussen vid Slussen.* — He got on the bus at Slussen.
*Jag kom på en idé.* — I came up with an idea.
*Hon hälsar på mig.* — She says hello to me. (*på* unstressed)
*Vi hälsar på dem.* — We're visiting them. (stress on *på*)

blocks.text: Sometimes a particle verb is perfectly logical: *gå ut* is "go out", *komma in* is "come in" — the particle just shows the direction. Sometimes it's pure idiom: nothing about *tycka* (think) and *om* (about) tells you that together they mean "like". Treat the idiomatic ones as new words, not as sums of their parts.

blocks.title: Ten particle verbs for every day
items: **stänga av** — turn off · **sätta på** — turn on
**ta på sig** — put on · **ta av sig** — take off

blocks.text: Every Swede knows the saying ***Det finns inget dåligt väder, bara dåliga kläder*** — "There's no such thing as bad weather, only bad clothes." Parents say it to children every winter morning. Dian is about to find out that it's mostly true.

Then make each one negative and polite: *Glöm inte att stänga av radion!*
